title: The canopy
hook: the wedding canopy is a new home, open on every side like Abraham's tent
carry: a house open on all sides

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tena'im, and your line was conditions: terms said out loud before the building starts. What plan did you make? Today, the building itself, and it has no walls. Day one thousand three hundred five.

A pole at each corner. A cloth across the top. That's all. No walls, no door, no lock. Sometimes the cloth is a prayer shawl that belonged to a grandparent; sometimes it's embroidered, or plain white, or a quilt friends stitched together. At some weddings, friends hold the poles up by hand, and you can see their arms get tired. The couple walks in, and the wind comes straight through. This little shelter is where a Jewish wedding happens. Why would a wedding happen in a room you can't close?
screen: `A POLE AT EACH CORNER, ONE CLOTH.` → `NO WALLS, NO DOOR.` → `WHY A ROOM YOU CAN'T CLOSE?`

segments.voice: Chuppah. The canopy. Turn it four ways. First, the word in the Bible. In Psalm nineteen, the sun rises across the sky like a groom. The King James puts it this way: "as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber." The Hebrew for that chamber is a form of chuppah. In the Bible it is a wedding room. At a Jewish wedding the room has shrunk to a cloth on poles, but it keeps its meaning. Second, a new home. The couple stands under it together, and tradition treats the chuppah as their first shared home, before there's a lease or a key. Being brought under it is part of what makes them married. Third, the open sides. Genesis tells of Abraham sitting "in the tent door in the heat of the day." He sees strangers coming and runs to meet them, with water for their feet and bread. The midrash adds a detail the verse doesn't: Abraham's tent had openings on every side, so travelers from any direction would find a door facing them. The chuppah, some teachers say, carries that tent into every wedding. A Jewish home is meant to be open to guests from the very first minute. Fourth, what holds it up. It's only cloth. A gust can lift it. When friends hold the poles, the picture is plain: a new home stands because the people around it keep it standing. A house open on all sides is a house that needs, and welcomes, everyone nearby.
screen: `A WEDDING ROOM IN THE PSALMS.` · `THE COUPLE'S FIRST HOME.` · `ABRAHAM'S TENT, OPEN EVERY WAY.` · `HELD UP BY FRIENDS.` · then, large: `A HOUSE OPEN ON ALL SIDES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand under something open. If you can, move under a doorway, a tree, a porch roof, or the plain sky. If you can't move, look up at the ceiling and then out toward the nearest window. Breathe. Let your home come to mind, whatever it is right now. If every side of it had a door, who would walk in? Who is already welcome? Who could be, if you opened one more side? Let one name come, and hold it gently. The bell holds the time.
Chuppah: the wedding canopy. A first home, with a roof and no walls, open like Abraham's tent. Today's word.
Your line: a house open on all sides. Today, open one side of your life to someone: an invitation, a seat at your table, a door left open. Day one thousand three hundred five.

howItsDone: A Jewish wedding takes place under a chuppah, a canopy of cloth on poles, sometimes a prayer shawl, sometimes held by friends; the couple stands beneath it as their first shared home.

original.note: Hebrew: canopy, the wedding room; Ashkenazi Jews often say KHOO-pah.

The midrash of Abraham's tent open on all sides: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 7 (and Bereshit Rabbah 48:9). Confirm the citation.
'Tradition treats the chuppah as their first shared home' and 'being brought under it is part of what makes them married' (chuppah as part of nissu'in); confirm the framing.
